summary: The fourth-largest island country in the world, located in the southwest Indian Ocean. Owing to long geographic isolation it has a great many endemic species (such as lemurs), and its inhabitants have both Southeast Asian and East African ancestry.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: In 1818 Welsh missionaries of the London Missionary Society arrived in the Merina Kingdom, founded schools and translated the Bible into Malagasy. Queen Ranavalona I (reigned 1828–1861) severely persecuted Christians, but in 1869 Ranavalona II was baptized and declared Protestantism the state religion, making Protestantism widespread among the Merina of the central highlands. Today the largest Protestant church is the Church of Jesus Christ in Madagascar (FJKM).

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism was introduced on the southern coast by French missionaries in the 17th century, but its influence was limited. After France colonized Madagascar in 1896, the Catholic Church expanded rapidly with the support of the colonial government, especially establishing schools and churches among the Betsileo of the center and in coastal areas. Today Catholic and Protestant strength are comparable.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs (ancestor worship)
ranking.description: Malagasy people generally believe that the spirits of ancestors (razana) influence the living, and although many are Christians, they still take part in ancestor-worship rituals such as the famadihana (turning of the bones). Those who follow only traditional religion are mainly in rural areas of the south and west.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Those who explicitly call themselves non-religious are mainly some residents of cities, but religion and belief in ancestors are widespread in Malagasy society, and relatively few people have no belief affiliation at all.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam arrived with Arab and Swahili traders on the northwestern coast in the Middle Ages, in port cities such as Mahajanga. Today Muslims include some Malagasy of the northwest, immigrants from the Comoros, and communities of Indian and Pakistani merchants who arrived in the 19th–20th centuries.

religion.background: The ancestors of the Malagasy crossed the Indian Ocean from the area of Borneo in Southeast Asia about 1,000–2,000 years ago, and later Bantu people from East Africa also moved in, forming a traditional belief centered on ancestor worship, such as the "famadihana". Islam arrived with Arab and Swahili traders on the northwestern coast in the Middle Ages. From 1818 missionaries of the London Missionary Society preached in the Merina Kingdom, and in 1869 Queen Ranavalona II was baptized and declared Protestantism the state religion. After French colonization in 1896 Catholicism expanded greatly. Today most people are Christian, but ancestor worship still runs in parallel with Christianity.

language.official: The official languages are Malagasy and French.

ranking.name: Malagasy
ranking.description: Malagasy is the common language of the whole island; although there are different dialects in different places, they basically all derive from a single Austronesian language. From the 1820s missionaries established a written standard based on the Merina dialect; after independence Malagasy became the national language, and in the 1970s "Malagasization" was promoted to replace French-language education, so almost all citizens have it as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: During French colonial rule (1896–1960) French was the official and educational language, and after independence it remained an important language of government, higher education and business. However, those who use French as their main language are only the urban elite, and most rural residents have limited French ability.

language.history: Malagasy belongs to the Austronesian language family and is closest to the Maanyan language of southeastern Borneo, which shows that the ancestors of the Malagasy crossed the Indian Ocean from Southeast Asia about 1,000–2,000 years ago; it also absorbed vocabulary from Bantu languages, Arabic, French and English. In early times the southwest wrote it in the Arabic script (called sorabe). In the 1820s missionaries of the London Missionary Society, in cooperation with Merina King Radama I, devised the Malagasy orthography in the Latin alphabet. During French colonial rule (1896–1960) French became the language of administration and education. After independence in 1960 Malagasy became the national language, and the 2010 constitution made Malagasy and French the official languages.

ranking.name: Romazava (Malagasy beef and greens stew)
ranking.description: A clear stew of zebu beef slowly cooked with local leafy greens (such as brèdes mafana, which numb the tongue), eaten with white rice.
ranking.history: Romazava is regarded as the national dish of Madagascar; "ro" in Malagasy refers to the broth that accompanies rice, reflecting the rice-centered food culture of the Malagasy. Madagascar is the African country where the most rice is eaten per person, and its rice culture comes from the traditions of its Southeast Asian ancestors. The zebu is a symbol of wealth in Malagasy society, so romazava with beef is often made at festivals and when entertaining guests.

ranking.name: Ravitoto (cassava leaves with pork)
ranking.description: Cassava leaves are pounded and slowly stewed with pork, with garlic and coconut milk added, and eaten with white rice. It has a thick texture with the distinctive aroma of cassava leaves and the richness of pork.
ranking.history: Cassava was introduced to Madagascar by Europeans in the 18th–19th centuries via East Africa and Indian Ocean trade; it is drought-tolerant and high-yielding, and its leaves are also eaten as a vegetable. Ravitoto means "pounded leaves", and traditionally women pound the leaves with a wooden mortar. It is one of the most popular home-style dishes in Madagascar and is especially common in the central highlands.

ranking.name: Mofo gasy (Malagasy rice cakes)
ranking.description: Small round rice cakes made from rice flour, coconut milk and sugar, baked in a special iron mold with round holes, crisp outside and soft inside. Lightly sweet, they are a common breakfast snack.
ranking.history: Mofo gasy means "Malagasy bread", to distinguish it from the baguette brought by the French in the colonial period (mofo vazaha, "foreigners' bread"). It is made from rice, continuing the rice-eating culture of the Southeast Asian ancestors, and resembles Southeast Asian rice cakes. In the early morning street vendors bake mofo gasy over charcoal fires, and it is eaten with coffee for breakfast, one of the most common street scenes in Madagascar.

ranking.name: Koba (banana and peanut cake)
ranking.description: An elongated sweet cake of rice flour, peanuts, banana and sugar mixed, wrapped in banana leaves and steamed for a long time. It has a dense, sweet texture with the aroma of peanuts and banana.
ranking.history: Koba is a traditional snack of the central highlands of Madagascar, and the practice of wrapping it with rice and banana leaves reflects the food traditions of the Southeast Asian ancestors, resembling Southeast Asian zongzi-like foods. Peanuts are a crop that became widespread after the colonial period. It is often sold in slices in markets and is a treat at festivals and family gatherings.

ranking.name: Zebu beef
ranking.description: The meat of the zebu (humped cattle), eaten grilled, stewed or made into dried meat. The meat is fairly lean and has a distinctive flavor.
ranking.history: Zebu were brought to Madagascar by East African migrants about a thousand years ago and quickly became the most important livestock on the island. In Malagasy society the zebu is not only food but a symbol of wealth, status and bride price; at important ceremonies such as circumcisions, weddings, funerals and the famadihana, zebu are slaughtered as offerings to the ancestors and the meat is shared. In the south there is even a tradition of a coming-of-age ritual involving cattle raiding.
